subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION TO SETTLE STRIKE AT ST. JOHN'S AND MOUNT PEARL, NEWFOUNDLAND-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to move a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43 for which I ask the unanimous consent of the House. My motion is in connection with a serious situation at St. John's and Mount Pearl post offices in Newfoundland where members of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers went on strike last Monday afternoon at 3.20 p.m. and are continuing their strike despite the fact that a collective agreement is in force and the law prohibits such a strike during the term of an agreement. There are now some 12,000 unemployment insurance cheques totalling $2 million caught in the mail. Old age pensions, veterans cheques and social assistance cheques are scheduled to be delivered Monday but will be delayed if this strike continues. 1 therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka (Mr. Darling):
That this House urge the Postmaster General to use every possible means to bring this illegal work stoppage to a halt immediately by way of obtaining a court injunction or otherwise and urge the postal clerks involved to return to work so that the severe hardship caused members of the general public, including those dependent upon unemployment insurance cheques, old age security, veterans cheques and other social assistance cheques through the mails, will cease.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: EASTCAN EXPLORATION LIMITED-EXPLORATION OFF COAST OF LABRADOR
speechtext:
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources reports as follows: 1. In December Eastcan indicated to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources that it would be unable to continue drilling operations on its federal permits offshore from Labrador unless it received assurances from the Newfoundland Government that its interests offshore from Labrador would not be nullified or expropriated in the event that the province was successful in acquiring jurisdiction over the offshore areas involved as a result of the forthcoming agreed joint Reference to the Supreme Court of Canada. On Janaury 31 of this year the company advised the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources that it was now in receipt of draft regulations prepared by the Newfoundland Government and, while the company could not discuss their content, it was of the view it could not proceed with this year's drilling program on the basis of those regulations.
2.	A Minister of the Federal Crown requires no authorization from the private sector to make public satements.
3.	The group of companies of which Total Eastcan Exploration Ltd. is a partner in respect of federal oil and gas rights offshore from Newfoundland and Labrador has indicated in discussions with federal authorities that it would be prepared to continue drilling operations on these rights if the Newfoundland Government provided the assurances referred to in the response to Question 1. This would indicate that the group considers that the provisions of the proposed federal regulations that have been made public are not such as to inhibit the companies involved from undertaking the heavy investments necessary to conduct oil and gas drilling operations offshore from Labrador.
4.	Yes. (a) The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has spoken with Premier Moores and also sent him a telex to endeavour to initiate discussions leading to a resolution of the problem, (b) Not applicable, pending results of discussions referred to in (a).

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON UNIFIED FAMILY COURT PROJECT IN NEWFOUNDLAND AND PAST AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
1. The Minister of Justice met with the Attorney General for Newfoundland, in St. John's Newfoundland, March 4, 1977. Following their meeting the ministers issued a joint announcement that they had agreed to the establishing of an experimental Unified Family court project for the St. John's area. The ministers noted in their announcement that the establishment of the experimental Unified Family Court project is contingent upon agreement between the federal and provincial governments on certain specific details.
2.	While specific details as to the distribution of costs have yet to be decided upon, it was agreed that the costs of the experiment are to be shared by both governments. Vote number 10 of the Department of Justice set out in the estimates for the fiscal period ending March 31, 1978 provides for contributions for pilot projects relating to family courts throughout Canada in the total amount of $350,000.
3.	At present the government has entered into negotiations for Unified Family Courts in the provinces of Ontario, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. While agreement in principle has been reached in Manitoba and Ontario, no formal agreement for joint funding of a Unified Family Court pilot project has yet been entered into by the Minister of Justice and the Attorney General of a province. Some funds have been expended, however, to pay for the joint funding of the evaluation of the unified family court pilot project commenced by British Columbia in 1974.

speechtext:
Order, please. At this stage of the metric conversion bill there are for consideration at the report stage eight motions, seven of which stand in the name of the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil). Of those, six-in the opinion of the Chair-have basically the same intent and, therefore, subject to any suggestions to the contrary, could be grouped together both for discussion and vote. I refer to motions 1, 2, 4, 5, 7 and 8 standing in the name of the hon. member for Moose Jaw. Unless it is otherwise suggested, they could be grouped together for discussion. I might be persuaded, if there is some necessity to split them for the purpose of voting, so to do. If that seems necessary, or if that necessity develops during the course of discussion, then certainly representations could be entertained about splitting them if the House is of such disposition.
Motion No. 3, in the name of the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) should be debated and voted on separately. Motion No. 6, in the name of the hon. member for Moose Jaw, has a different intent and ought to be discussed and voted on separately. Unless during the course of discussion some indication to the contrary develops, perhaps the House is prepard to proceed with the discussion and disposition of the motions as I have proposed. If so, I would now call for consideration the six motions previously referred to standing in the name of the hon. member for Moose Jaw.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak on the motions I have placed before the House. There is deep concern among western farmers about conversion to the metric system. Frankly, I sympathize with the minister because I think he has been mesmerized, and possibly misled, by the Metric Commission which led him to believe that western producers and farmers unanimously favoured the metric system. Even a member from western Canada, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) was of the same conviction. On second reading, he said in this House on January 26, as reported on page 2422 of Hansard'.
1 want to deal with a few of the aspects of metric conversion affecting grain which may not be fully appreciated but upon the basis of which I believe this measure is not only supportable but is also in the best long-run interests of all segments of the grains industry, including producers in the prairie region. First, it should be noted that this change has a broad and virtually unanimous base of support in the farm community.
That is just not so. Western farmers are almost unanimously opposed to the metric system. How did the minister come to that conclusion? The Metric Commission, a group of bureaucrats, set up what they called a subcommittee, the Canadian bulk grain handling committee. Who was on that committee? It is interesting to read the organizations represented on that commission. We start off with a representative from the Canadian Grain Commission, the Canadian Feed Manufacturers' Association, the Canada Grains Council, the Pioneer Grain Company Limited, the Alberta Wheat Pool, the United Grain Growers, the Canadian Wheat Board, the Ontario Grain and Feed Dealers Association, the Alberta Wheat Pool, again, the Canadian Grain Commission, again, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, the Anglo-Canadian Grain Company, the Department of Agriculture for the province of Saskatchewan and a co-ordinator from the Metric Commission.
Almost without exception each and every one of the organizations represented on that commission has a vested interest. Those people represent organizations which are in the grain handling industry. If you examine the list you will see there is not one producer represented on the committee, a committee
Metric System
presumably set up to advise the Metric Commission, which in turn will advise the minister. The minister was not at the committee hearings, but possibly he read the reports of the standing committee. If so, he will recall that the committee had representatives appear from various organizations. I will list them. They are the Canadian Wheat Board, the Farm Grain Services Union,. Unifarm, the Manitoba Farm Bureau, SARM, the Saskatchewan Urban Municipalities Association, and the NFU.
It is interesting to note that the representatives who appeared on behalf of the National Farmers Union did not come from western Canada, despite the fact there were some in this part of the country at the time. They sent the vice-president, who comes from Prince Edward Island, and a representative from the province of Ontario.
This bill has to do with producers in the Canadian Wheat Board area which, as hon. members know, is western Canada. It takes in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and part of the Peace River. The representatives of all the organizations which appeared, with the exception of the Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities and the Saskatchewan Association of Urban Municipalities, led the committee to believe that they represented the majority of the farmers in the west and that those whom they represented were in favour of metrication.

So there can be no doubt that the majority of farmers are opposed to the metric system. I think

it is safe to say that between 95 per cent and 100 per cent of the farmers in western Canada are opposed to metrification. But I would add this: farmers understand that the world is gradually converting to the metric system and that eventually we shall end up using a complete metric system in this country. However, they also know that such a decision has not yet been taken in the United States, and they feel that because of our close trade relationship with the United States any action we take should be in step with that taken by the Americans.
My amendments simply call upon the government, under the wheat stabilization legislation, under the program for cash advances for crops, under the two-price system for wheat, and so on, to use a dual system, a system which shows bushels, acres, tonnes and hectares. It is likely that the majority of the older farmers in the west, who have been accustomed to using bushels and acres all their lives, will continue to do so. But, as 1 say, they realize we have to progress and they say, "We shall progress; but take it in stages. Give us the opportunity to convert over the years by letting us have a dual system." Mr. Speaker, in nearly 20 years of being around the House I have never witnessed a more alarming and shocking thing than I have witnessed here today. The issue is very simple. It is no longer a matter of conversion to the metric system; it is a matter of how, in a democratic system, we represent our people. We are dealing today with a series of amendments to Bill C-23. I have nothing against the metric system, but I suggest a more humane method of putting it into effect in order to allow the people to adjust without too much hardship in terms of time or money; that is all.
Evidence was given to us in the committee by representatives of grain companies, the National Farmers Union, union spokesmen for elevator men in the west, consumers, and so on. We heard from those who have a vested interest, and by that I mean those who will lose or make money out of the idea. The government says it wants metric conversion as it is laid down in this bill, and the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) said flatly this morning-and there has been no contradiction of his statement-that the great majority of the people affected by this legislation have expressed opposition to it. We in this House are saying that since the metric system is a better system than the imperial system, parliament arbitrarily should ram it down the throats of our people without even listening to their protests and arguments.
I do not use that expression very often. In all the years I have been here it has never been clearer to me than it is now that on the very fundamentals of how we serve our people we are alienating them from the institution of parliament. All we hear in the media today is that Quebec has a problem, or that western Canada has a problem, but we know that in every part of Canada and in every segment of our population people are showing signs of distress-"alienation" is the big word for it-

March 25, 1977
Metric System
over how their institutions are looking after them. They feel they no longer have any say.
I have always supported the concept that sooner or later we should change to the metric system because it is more convenient and better arithmetically, but never have I advocated something which, even though better for us in the long run, would do harm to our people now without making that suggestion as humanely as possible.
The amendments moved by the hon. member for Moose Jaw simply provide a method of moving less quickly into the metric system. We are trying to rush conversion through without the consent of the people, and arousing their animosities because of the cost and inconvenience of adopting a new system. We are arousing their deeper instinct that they are being overrun by their own legislators. That latter fear is a deep great one in Canada. We are going against all the rules of democratic procedures, because the evidence is very clear that 95 per cent to 97 per cent of the rank and file of farm organizations are against what is happening here. But the minister states that we have to accept the word of the executives of grain companies. That is the issue.
I do not believe we have to call a referendum on this subject, although that is proposed in many letters which I have. I think that the common sense of hon. members in this chamber should be such that we should do what is most acceptable. It is very clear to every hon. member of this House, whether on the government side or on this side, that the people directly affected-in this case, mostly the farmers of western Canada but also the consumers of Canada-have expressed in the only way they know, by official resolutions passed by their organizations and letters to their members of parliament, that they are opposed. I do not think the members of this chamber should say "To heck with them. We are going to ram it through". That is the essence of the reason I am supporting the amendments moved by the hon. member for Moose Jaw which simply propose that we use both measurements.
The Canadian Wheat Board, always aware of the fact that it is held responsible for its behaviour by farmers, recognized this immediately and accepted the proposal. The minister has expressed in the House that the Canadian Wheat Board is going to use both systems on its forms. So here we have one so-called institution of this parliament saying that in spite of this legislation it is going to allow all wheat farmers to use both systems on their forms. When we pass this legislation, as the government wishes us to do, I question whether the Canadian Wheat Board will be acting within the law because the law will provide that only one system be used. However, because the Canadian Wheat Board is an independent board I suppose it will ignore the law because it has the support of the minister.
Under this legislation, only the metric system is to be used. The minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board argued today that this does not affect land measurement. Such errant nonsense as that statement rarely comes into this House. The federal Metric Commission went to the provinces and said that this is the law at the federal level and the

provinces should harmonize their legislation with that law. The provinces were conned into believing that this was the law and that this parliament had passed it. But that was not the case. Before metric conversion is complete, 90 statutes of this parliament will have to be amended. The bill before us proposes amending nine of those 90, so I suggest the statement that the provincial governments have responsibility for land measurement begs the question. If the Metric Commission told the provincial governments that that was the law, and that the provinces would have to pass laws to harmonize with it, the federal government would have to accept responsibility for that.
Metric conversion, as it applies to land measurement, will have serious repercussions. When people in the cities of Saskatchewan have their lots measured, they will have to get them accurately surveyed in the metric system before they can be registered at the land titles office. That means money for lawyers and money for surveyors. As everyone knows, our roads system is based on the mile; our land measurements are based on the mile. The British democracy allows its people to keep the mile, but apparently in Canada we are not going to have that right because the public service bureaucracy has decided to confuse us.
The federal bureaucracy, working in harmony with the bureaucracies of the provinces, has decided that the metric system must be rammed down our throats immediately. The essence of the issue is bringing the metric system to North America and Australia which are the only remaining parts of the world which do not use the metric system. It can be done quickly, as it was done in Australia, or it can be done gradually as it is being done in Great Britain and in the United States.
I would like to bring to the attention of this House the comparison which exists between the democractic country of the United States and the once democractic country of Canada.
I have here a letter from the Committee on Science and Technology of the United States House of Representatives describing how metric conversion will work in that country. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), to whom the letter is addressed, has referred to it already in this House so I will just read the relevant paragraph. The letter is signed by a member of the Congress, Don Fuqua, and the relevant paragraph reads as follows:
The first and perhaps most important aspect of the American law is that no one will be asked to change to the metric system unless it is done voluntarily. The Act specifically provides that the United States Metric Board "shall have no compulsory powers."
The matter of land measurements was specifically discussed in our committee hearings. Land measurement was frequently given as an example where there would be very little advantage to be gained from making the changeover and where the costs of doing so would be entirely out of proportion to any possible gains. It was also noted that in the State of Louisiana land measurements continue to be made in the old French measurements, a leftover from the days when France colonized that part of the continent. The same applies to Spanish land measurements in California. In neither of these cases has it been found
March 25, 1977

advantageous to switch to the English system in the past, and there are not now any plans to switch those measurements or any land measurements elsewhere in the United States to metric measurements.
If, in changing over to the metric system, the United States wants to do it slowly and on a voluntary basis, and if Australia wants to ram it through, then which example should Canada follow? I contend we should support the amendments before us as moderate, positive proposals put forward by the official opposition. In a democratic country where the people have made it clear where they stand, these things should be done in the way that would cause least hardship. These amendments simply call for a permissive or dual system. The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board should speak for the farmers of the west and support our proposals instead of saying what he did this morning. The minister knows that he has not been correctly informed, either by his officials or by the people who gave evidence before the standing committee. I know the seriousness of the charge I now make, Mr. Speaker.
It is disgraceful that organizations such as the Saskatchewan Pool and the Manitoba Pool, which call themselves democratic, should be pressuring the government to pass a law at this time which is to their financial advantage and is not in the interests of their members. The membership has never been given a chance to express its views on this subject.
At meetings at the local committee level, the subdistrict level and district level, resolutions have been passed and sent to the head office. Having these in his possession the secretary of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool had the colossal effrontery to write to the minister saying that in the years 1974, 1975 and 1976 no resolutions were passed by any of the 800 committees in Saskatchewan. This left the impression that all committees were in favour of the pool's stand when at that time he had in his possession official, signed resolutions from six separate areas in Saskatchewan, which represents a large proportion of the people in the province, to the contrary. We cannot do anything about this sort of thing here in parliament; it is up to members of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool to deal with the people they elect, and it is up to the elected officials to deal with those they appoint and pay. I think it is a shame that in a so-called democratic system like Saskatchewan this type of thing is going on.
I have many letters here, Mr. Speaker, but one really hits me hard. It is on the stationery of the Manitoba Pool Elevators, signed by the general manager, and addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). It urges the government to bring metric conversion into effect rapidly. One paragraph reads as follows:
If the conversion to metric tonnes does not take place quickly we fear it will be impossible to generate any enthusiasm for implementation at a later date because there will always be a danger that instructions will again be changed.
What does that mean, Mr. Speaker? They realize that once the farmers know they will be given a chance to decide this thing, they will not accept it. This type of attitude toward their own members is something that the Manitoba Pool organization and the Saskatchewan Pool organization will have to settle. It is not our task to interfere. We can point out, as we have done, that it is almost a question of privilege for this
Metric System
House when this type of information is sent to a minister and a Prime Minister. As a member from Saskatchewan I am quite willing to fight this issue throughout the province. I know how it will go because members of all organizations in Saskatchewan hate to be pushed around, by their own organization or by this parliament.
In these amendments we are specifically concerned with five bills that deal with the handling of grain in the west. I appeal to members of all political persuasions in this House to put democracy in the forefront of their decision-making. If civil servants are trying to push something through just because Australia has done it that way, they should be fired and told who is boss. If farm organizations and grain companies apply political pressure, they should be told that it is the rank and file who have the power and they will be listened to. I urge members to speak as parliamentarians. This is not a question of conscience; it is a question of moral judgment. Is it right to ignore the expressed wishes of the rank and file affected by this legislation? I am talking now about the western farmer who is the person concerned in the amendment before us.
I appeal also to my friends from Quebec. The land system in Quebec is not measured in acres, it is in arpents. When the time comes when they try to force farmers to change from arpents to hectares, there will be a battle. The whole trouble started in Ottawa when they tried to persuade Quebec to adopt metric conversion on a crash basis.
The question is simply whether we crash this thing through without any regard for the people affected, or whether we give them an alternative system to follow until they get used to the new system.
At the beginning of second reading debate I suggested that if the word "hectares" were removed from the bill we would pass it that afternoon and help persuade farmers that, if they accepted tonnes, we would protect them against change in land measurements. I thought the government had reacted favourably to that, and that is why we let the debate drop and the bill go to committee. But the minister came to committee and repudiated what I thought was an understanding. Apparently the civil servants felt that it would confuse Canadians to have two systems simultaneously. They have two systems in the United States; they have them in Great Britain. Are we stupid? Can we not get along with two systems?

... The Robsart Wheat Pool Committee held a committee meeting in the elevator office on the evening of February 8, with our delegates ...
A good discussion was had in regards to the metric system and the conversion consequences. It was generally agreed that the metric conversion is not going to be readily accepted by farmers and that the measurements by bushels and acres should be retained. The committee felt that it was absolutely absurd to resurvey the land for hectares. After all, that would not change the actual quarters or sections and it would certainly cost the country millions of dollars. That isn't necessary.

Resolution-Moved . . . seconded .. . that the metric system does not convert to tonnes or hectares in the agricultural sector for the many reasons as stated above. Carried.
The letter is signed by Howard Olson, secretary of the Robsart Wheat Pool Committee.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext:
motion No. 3:
That Bill C-23, an act to facilitate conversion to the metric system of measurement, be amended in clause 3 at page 2 by adding immediately after line 12 the following new subclause:
"(3) This section shall come into force on the first day of March 1980."
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion just moved in my name was proposed in the standing committee by the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling). I point out that motion No. 3 has little to do with the Wheat Board. If passed it would affect all consumers across Canada. It seeks to amend clause 3, which mentions the Packaging and Labelling Act,
March 25, 1977

and the Weights and Measures Act. Clearly this matter is of concern to all consumers in Canada.
At present it is legal and proper to print on a package or label both the imperial and the metric measure of the contents of the package. For example, almost every person in every household in Canada has been to a store to buy a half gallon carboard carton of milk. The language on two sides is French, and on two sides English. At the bottom of the carton you see the expression, "one half gallon", and beside it the figure of "2.27 litres". If people prefer their measurements in litres they know exactly how much they are getting, 2.27 litres. Similarly those used to the imperial measurement know they are getting a half gallon. But the legislation now before the House would make it illegal to measure milk by the half gallon. You will be able to use only the 2.27 litres measurement. Manufacturers will be able to round off the numbers, to make the measurement either 2 litres or 4 litres.
You will never again see units of imperial measurement on any package in Canada. That is what clause 3 will do. Some of us do not like that kind of doctrinaire, dictatorial approach. We think that people used to the half gallon measurement will be confused. Why should that volume be measured only as 2.27 litres? You can bet your bottom dollar that no manufacturer who has millions of dollars worth of these little cardboard cartons stacked up in his warehouse will burn them and put out a new carton for two litres. He will use the old cartons. When you get a new carton, it will be 2.27 litres.
I am simply putting forward in a very simple way what this clause does. A farmer buying feed for his chickens used to buy it in 50 pound containers. Now it will be in some other measure, 25 kilograms I think it is. The equivalent is not the same, so it will lead to confusion. For years turkey and chicken farmers have bought feed in 50 pound bags. Now they will see pasted over the side a great strip which states so many kilograms.
One farmer who was always a bit cautious picked up a bag. He had been picking up bags for years. He put it on the scale because it looked the same as the old size bag he had always bought. Instead of having a 50 pound figure on it, it indicated so many kilograms. He weighed the bag and what did he find? Did he find 56 pounds which should be in there because that is equal to the number of kilograms and he has learned to multiply by 2.2? He finds the same 50 pounds of chicken feed but he is charged for 55 or 56 pounds. This is what happens during the switchover.
No manufacturer of bags for chicken feed will change the size of the bag because some government comes along and says he must use only the metric system. He just pastes a little strip on the outside and puts on it the metric measurement. However, he does not change the quantity in the bag.
The merchant in the store tells the farmer that he has so many kilograms. If it turns out to be 25 kilograms or something like that and the farmer protests he is not getting the right amount, the only thing I can do when I receive a letter
Metric System
from him is to turn that over to the Department of Consumer Affairs and ask that it be checked out. They will have to hire an army of inspectors as big as the civil service in order to track down all these complaints across the country.
In essence, what the amendment says is that you wait a little while before you enforce this amendment. The date suggested is 1980. It states that clause 3 on page 2 be amended by adding thereto the following subsection:
(3) This section shall come into force on the first day of March 1980.
Why 1980? If you look through all this literature, that is about the date the Americans and their industry will be moving in that direction. You give the consumer, every store and every plant in Canada three years to get used to the new terms such as kilograms, grams and so on.
This is a moderate constructive amendment. It was asked for by the Consumers Association of Canada. I cannot say they asked all of their people where they stand on this so I do not know how the consumers do stand. However, the association which made this presentation to the committee said this is what they would like, that it would give some time to get used to it. It fits in with the philosophy I mentioned on second reading debate.
Please, as we bring this metric system in, make it as humane as possible. There are those whose eyesight is not good enough to read what is on a package, but they are used to a size. Even though their eyes are not good, they can recognize a half gallon container. However, if they have to read 2.27 litres, they may not be able to make that out. I simply say on behalf of those who have poor eyesight, be humane and let them have a familiar size package, which will be continued anyway. Do not force them to accept the newer size package too quickly.
Second, there are those who have difficulty in translating from one type of system to another. I know that for the smart guys of the world, when they see a package of 400 grams, it is easy for them. They know that 400 grams is four tenths of a kilogram and a kilogram is 2.2 pounds so four tenths of 2.2 pounds is .88 of a pound, something less than a pound. With this skill to translate, you know that when you see 400 grams, it is something less than a pound. However, there may be a few people in Canada who will have trouble with that conversion.
All this amendment asks is to please let the thing go as it is now with both on the package. I do not buy small things which are packaged in millilitres or smaller units than the gram, but I suggest this type of amendment would not hurt the conversion to the metric system one bit. Simply let the packaging continue as it is today with both measurements. We insist that French and English be on the package. Why not let the imperial system stay there along with the metric system for three years? That is the heart and gist of this amendment.
I do not know how many consumers there are in Canada. There are 23 million people and they are probably all consumers. I suppose about one quarter of them do the shopping. On behalf of the five million people who do the shopping, whether they are male or female, I ask the House to accept this amendment which in no way interferes with conversion to the

March 25, 1977
Metric System
metric system. Let us have the two units on the package until the year 1980. Is that too much to ask on behalf of all the consumers? I do not think so.
I suspect, however, that the government whip has been laid on. These members have been told that if they accept this amendment, they will be in trouble with civil servants who do not like any deviation from the norm. I ask hon. members once again, stand up as individuals representing the people of your constituencies and express your will. I want to see the names in the recorded votes of Hansard so that people will know how they vote on this issue on behalf of the consumers of Canada.
I want to know whether the people who call themselves the members of the government, living in a free society, are prepared to go back in and say they do not give a hoot what you think, it is what we think that counts. I want to know because this whole issue has not developed as a debate on whether to convert to the metric system. It has developed into a clear cut example of the bureaucracy running governments at both the federal and provincial levels and members not being man enough or woman enough to stand up against it.
I would like to see this amendment accepted with good heart. All it asks is that we give the consumer three years to adjust as a measure of humanity toward our fellow man.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few brief remarks with respect to this amendment. In committee we had the privilege of hearing representations from the Consumers Association of Canada. Their presentation was very straightforward. Part of it was an audio-visual presentation. They brought with them packages of certain goods and pointed out the problems that will occur if this piece of legislation passes. Just as an example they showed three packages, one of four ounces, one of eight ounces and one of 16 ounces and they showed that until such time as there was a standardization of containers or packaging, these particular packages would read 114 millilitres, 227 millilitres and 455 millilitres, or 113 grams, 227 grams and 454 grams. They were pointing out to the committee that it would be very difficult for a consumer going into a store where there was labelling only under the metric system and where there were not any even numbers, to do the necessary calculations. As they said, when you have four ounce, eight ounce and 16 ounce packages it is only a matter of doubling the price to see which is the best bargain, but when dealing with millilitres or grams it is almost impossible to make the calculation unless you have a pencil and paper or a pocket calculator. I would suspect that if and when this bill becomes law in its present form the calculator industry is really going to boom. Indeed, it might be advisable to buy shares in some of the companies which produce calculators because every farmer and every consumer will have to carry a calculator around in his pocket to do the necessary calculations. Something of that sort will be needed in order to determine the relationship between prices of goods and quantity he is buying, or the quantity of chemicals he must put on his land.

It is interesting to note what the Consumers Association of Canada have been saying on this subject. I would like to read a couple of paragraphs from the Association's presentation. Let me make it clear that the Consumers Association is not opposed to metrication but it is opposed to this particular clause which will, overnight, require labelling under the metric system only. This is what the Association said in committee:
CAC is entirely in favour of single metric labelling of grocery products but only when the industry has adopted a rationalized series of hard metric sizes ... We feel very strongly that metric-only should occur when a product has moved into a standard metric size. It has been proven in other countries that the consumer relies on the old size and does not look at the new, if the change has been made, so there is no learning process. But we are against having the single metric-only for products which have not experienced conversion to metric.
Then they go on to say:
It is the position of the Association that removal of dual labelling requirements from the Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act, as envisaged in clause three of this bill, with the result that any manufacturer will be able to label any size of grocery product in metric only, is premature and can only lead to confusion and consumer abuses in the marketplace.
Representatives of the Consumers Association were in attendance before the committee when the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) presented this amendment which has the effect of requiring dual labelling until 1980. They agreed with the amendment. They said it was the type of amendment they wanted, because by 1980 packages would have been standardized. It was interesting to observe what happened in that committee. Government members sat back while the witnesses were in attendance and when the amendment was discussed. What did they say? They said, when it came to the amendment which dealt with acres and hectares, that they could not accept it because the farm organizations had come before the committee, stating that they represented the farmers of Western Canada, and that those farmers wanted to go metric. On that basis they turned down our amendment. The suggestion was that we, in the opposition, did not understand what the people of Western Canada wanted.
What happened when the representatives of the Consumers Association came before the committee? In the same way, they said they represented consumers-I think they said they represented 100,000 consumers across Canada. That is a large number. But what was the reaction of hon. members on the government side? They said, in effect: We are not going to believe the representatives of the consumers of Canada and we shall not accept the amendment. So on one hand there is a situation in which government members believed members of associations, which said they represented farmers and on the other hand a situation where apparently they did not believe an association which represents a very large number of Canadian consumers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it certainly gives me pleasure to speak on this motion for the simple reason that I represent an area of Canada where there is very little newspaper coverage, very little television coverage, very little radio coverage, and the people of this area have really not been kept up to date as to what is happening with metric conversion.
With regard to weather conditions, people seemed to manage quite well over the past hundred years or so, being able to determine the temperature or the weather by using the Fahrenheit system. But now that we have gone to the metric system and all the reports are given in that system no one knows what the weather is going to be like.
With regard to labelling produce in a certain type of container with both metric and conventional measurement, this will be confusing to people in the north. This is particularly so when the price of articles in expensive; people will not know whether they are being ripped off by the merchant. I think the people in the north are just not ready for this. Not enough education has been given these people on this measure, and it will only confuse them. Therefore when we vote on this motion on Monday I hope it will be carried. We must think of those who are not exposed to the media in the same way as those who live in the great corridor between Montreal and Windsor.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation whatever in supporting this motion to delay this move until 1980.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on rising to speak to this motion on metric conversion may I say at the outset that I do so more from confusion than anything else. Metric conversion is new to many people in Canada, and I am not ashamed or afraid to say that I will experience a totally new learning process myself. I am not alone in this; I believe a large percentage of the population are in the same position.
Metric System
Clause 3 provides for metric labelling, and our party has moved a motion to provide that we go slow on this until 1980. In other words, we will then have some length of time to undergo the learning process which many of us will have to go through.
I am sure most members of the House know that we have a lot in common with the United States so far as imports and exports are concerned. However, it appears to me that the situation concerning metric labelling will be similar to that of bilingual labelling. We do not know exactly when the act is going to be proclaimed, or whether only certain sections at a time will be proclaimed. Would the hon. member like to listen for a moment? We are having a hard enough time in Canada today, what with unemployment, and with helping businesses in Canada get started. There are all kinds of trade barriers. There is no free trade or fair trade; instead we have unfair trade barriers between our two countries. The same thing happens to our exporters. So far as the lumber industry in British Columbia is concerned, 62 per cent of our exports go to the United States. The lumber mills are not going to be able to put metric labels on their exports to the United States; they must label the product using the measurements used in the United States. Nevertheless, many companies in Canada will be required to put a dual label on their exports. One of the organizations I was very close to or was part of-indeed I still am-is the fruit industry of British Columbia. We sell a lot of our produce in the United States, and I think it is in the best interests of Canada that we continue to export our produce. The same is true of the lumber industry in British Columbia. This generates export dollars for Canada.
4362

March 25, 1977
Metric System
We import enough produce from the United States as it is now. The balance of trade in fruit and farm produce is almost equal; we maintain an equal balance over-all mainly because of our wheat exports. I did not think we will have to label every kernel of grain or boxcar of wheat, but owing to their size the containers in which produce is exported from Canada will have to be labelled.
Imports are still coming into Canada without a bilingual label. As I have said, businesses in Canada have been badgered, bullied, or whatever you want to call it, into putting bilingual labels on their products, in many instances at high cost. There will be all kinds of confusion as to how you label your product according to where it is going to or coming from. The whole thing will be confused. It will be a dog's breakfast. That is exactly what it will be.
We are offering an amendment to postpone this until 1980. No wonder the Consumers Association of Canada has taken a hard look at this. Mr. Speaker, I do not want to delay the proceedings on this very much. I would like to speak for about two minutes. The rapid march to the metric system appears to me to be out of step, unless it coincides with changes contemplated by our largest trading partner and our greatest supplier of imports, the United States of America. I suggest the hon. member's amendment will go a long way in assisting us in this regard. I want to speak just for a moment in support of it.
I am concerned about the great cooking recipes of all times. I am referring to the ones that came down to us from our grandmothers. There are very few among us who can translate them from ounces, cups, pinches and tablespoons to such enlightening things as litres, millilitres, and cubic centimetres. The result will not be as tasty. A cherry nut bread, a banana bread, or an apple pan dowdy will never be the same. One lady whom I have respected all my life said to me, "Why can't the government just leave us alone? They have changed our old traditions. They have watched our work ethic erode. Now they are imposing chaos for seniors in the market place."
I am not sure that it should happen, but if it must happen I strongly urge the House to do it in step with our American neighbours. I am very much concerned about the great seafood dishes from down east where I come from in Atlantic Canada. What will the metric system do to them? Who can translate those recipes into metric terms? I suggest that it is darn near impossible. I would like to see us move as slowly as we possibly can on this piece of legislation.

I have been concerned, as I am sure all members have, with the customs and the traditions of our law-shaping forces. As time moves on and our legislation becomes more mature and our system becomes more mature, the basic law-shaping forces are much more removed from their former functions. We have witnessed the rise of bureaucracy and the fact that bureaucracy is the principal law-shaping force in our land. I have found that the Canadian people I have talked to do not want this system. I do not think they understand it. I do not think enough has been done of an explanatory nature, although a great deal of money has been spent in this field. I find people asking themselves, "How do we participate in this democracy now?" Members of parliament are in Ottawa for nine months of the year. How do the average Canadians let us know they do not like this, and what they would like instead of it?
We should address ourselves to this question of participation. This is a darn good example. The people do not want this legislation. However, we are here and seem prepared to pass it. We are, in effect, saying to the Canadian people, "This is good for you and you darn well better have it." I am afraid if we keep on in this direction much longer that the Canadian people are going to tell us what is good for us. Some members who vote for this and ram it down their throats are going to regret it very much.

speechtext:
motion No. 6:
That Bill C-23, an act to facilitate conversion to the metric system of measurement, be amended in clause 6 by striking out lines 36 to 44 at page 4 and lines 1 to 25 at page 5.
March 25, 1977

He said: Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few brief comments in connection with this amendment. Basically it is part and parcel of the previous amendments on which we have spoken. It pertains to the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act and has to do with the calculations made thereunder. Basically the remarks that I made on the motions that were grouped together apply to this particular amendment.
I would like to make a comment with respect to a remark made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). He seemed to indicate that I was suggesting that this particular bill would change the land title systems in the provinces of western Canada. I, at no time, ever made such a remark. I realize that the land title systems in our country are within the jurisdiction of the provincial governments. What I have said in the past, and will repeat again, is that because of this legislation which, in effect, requires the farmer to make use of hectares and tonnes, it will create a pressure and has created a pressure on the provincial governments to make changes in their land title systems. For example, in the province of Saskatchewan they made changes in April or May of last year. It is interesting to note that these changes were not made by the legislature of that province. The members of the legislative assembly in Saskatchewan did not have a chance to debate any bill. The people in the province of Saskatchewan did not have the opportunity of any input into the change.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext: It is the new democracy.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext:
My colleague to my right says, "It is the new democracy". It appears that is the way we are moving. The changes in the province of Saskatchewan were all made by order in council. Most people are familiar with an order in council. It is a series of regulations made either by the cabinet, or by a cabinet minister and approved by the other members of cabinet, promulgated, put in the Gazette, and it becomes law. That is an example of what happened in the province of Saskatchewan. The reason it happened was because the legislators in that province did not understand or did not know what was happening. There were some communications from the bureaucrats in Ottawa to the bureaucrats in Regina. The bureaucrats in Regina came to the conclusion that the change to the metric system was law, so they went ahead and they passed the regulations.
I am quite satisfied that if such a change in our land title system had been put before the legislature in any province, and the people in the province had the opportunity to learn what was going on, they would make their wishes known loud and clear because the people on the prairies have grown up under a system which uses acres. The west was surveyed about 100 years ago using statute miles. We have townships, we have ranges, we have sections, half sections, and quarter sections, all based on the mile. All the roads in the west that run north and south are one mile apart, and the ones that run east and west are two miles apart.
Metric System
Every farmer knows what an acre of land is. He can walk out into a field and say, "That piece of land contains X number of acres". He can tell by looking at it. He knows, when he takes his combine or his seed drill out into the field which is measured in feet, and he goes down the side of that field or makes a round around the field, how many acres he has covered. But the government, in its wisdom, will change all that. It is saying to the farmer, "From now on you will record everything in hectares and use tonnes per acre. But it will not be any problem; it is just a matter of calculation." The farmer knows how complicated the calculation will be; he knows the problems with which he will be faced. That is why he has expressed his opinion loud and clear to members of parliament. That is why local community committees of some of the farm organizations have passed resolutions saying they do not wish to convert to the metric system.
I think the farm organizations now have the message, but unfortunately that message did not get through to the government, and I do not know why because it is a simple matter to go out west, walk down the street of any town, and ask a farmer what he thinks about the metric system. He will tell you. I suggest that you can walk down the streets in any towns on the prairies, and you can spend the day talking to farmers, and I doubt if you would find one individual who is in favour of the change to the metric system, because the change is unnecessary. We do not sell land on the international markets. It will not add $1 to the farmer's income. All it will do is to create problems for him; it is a nuisance. It can create more than problems; it can cost him money because if he makes a mistake in some of his calculations when he is working with herbicides, pesticides, or even seeds, it can damage his crop.
I am pleased that a vote on these amendments will not take place until Monday, and I hope that the minister who is piloting this bill through the House-as a matter of fact it is his first bill-will sit back over the weekend and give serious thought to it. Perhaps he will talk to some of his colleagues and make a few phone calls to some of the farm organizations. If he wants to call some individuals, I can give him some telephone numbers, not necessarily of people of my political faith but of farmers who know what is happening in a community. Then he would understand what the feeling is among the farmers in western Canada. I can only hope that he will undertake to do that, and that when he comes back on Monday he will give instructions to his colleagues to support not only the amendments with respect to the western farmer, but the amendment with respect to dual labelling.

Mr. Speaker, we have tried this afternoon as clearly and as emphatically as we can to impress government members with the importance of ignoring their own whip and their own civil servants and doing what is right. We are considering an amendment which, as the preceding speaker, the hon. member for Moose Jaw, has said, is part of a package. We are now dealing with western farmers. I think I can put this into a very simple phrase again.

I want to remind the committee that 200 years ago last year the Americans had a rebellion against their lawful ruler, the king and emperor of the United Kingdom. Last year in 1976 they celebrated the 200th anniversary of that rebellion against their king. The issue on which they fought at that time, if I remember it correctly, was: no taxation without representation. What we are witnessing here today is metrification without representation.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (METRIC CONVERSION) AMENDMENT ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO WHEAT BOARD ACT TO FACILITATE CONVERSION TO METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext:
If hon. members on the government side think really hard, as the thinkers' conference in Toronto is supposed to be doing today, they will realize it is not only the farmers in the west who will be in a state of alienation and rebellion, but also consumers from one end of the country to the other.
To make certain there is no misunderstanding about what the hon. member for Moose Jaw said, and what I tried to say earlier in the debate about the feeling of the farmers, this can all be verified. There was a meeting in Lethbridge, Alberta, two weeks ago called by the Canadian Wheat Board to discuss the pricing of wheat. The minister knows what I am talking about. Farmers are concerned that mistakes are being made in the pricing policy of the Wheat Board. Questions were asked about the metric system. At that meeting 1,100 to 1,200 farmers tried to get into the hall. There is interest out there. Only 800 were allowed in because the fire marshal said that that was all the hall could accommodate safely. When the chairman asked how many of those present were in favour of the metric system, out of the 800 farmers in that hall ten hands went up. When he asked how many were opposed, 790 farmers stood to their feet. If the farmers do not understand that type of arithmetic, the government should.
In the same province of Alberta at Indus, at a meeting of the Alberta pool, part of the agenda was that there was to be a film on the metric system. Delegates from every district of Alberta said, "Take that out of here", and they took it out, because when Alberta farmers say take something out, it is taken out.
Third, farm organizations and pools are generally associated with a great part of the area I represent. The towns of Indian Head, Sintaluta and Abernethy may not mean a thing to the generation which sits in this House now, but prairie farm organizations began in this area in the territorial days. This is the area which produced Motherwell and Jimmy Gardiner. Even I was asked to run. What do the people in this historic centre of farm revolt and fighting for farm freedom say? The telegram I have in my hand is dated February 10, and it says:
We the following are members of Sask. Wheat Pool and are opposed to the metric system being brought into effect for grain and acres without farmers' agreement.
This telegram is signed by Don Woods, secretary of the wheat pool; A1 Guest, Albert Gares, Gordon Barber, E. Smithson and Alf Goodwin. These people are all from Indian Head.

It is also signed by Dave Mercer from Lemberg, Jimmy Gardiner's old home town; G. R. Pollock, Sintaluta, the home of the United Grain Growers farm movement; Richard Barnsley of Abernethy, the home of Motherwell. In a postscript the telegram says the following:
No mention was made at the pool's annual meeting regarding opposition or agreement to the metric system. I believe we have been misled in believing that it had already been made law.
I read those names because those names are known to every farmer in that big grain growing area in my constituency.
Fourth, I asked an old grain man from the southern part of my constituency along the American border to find out what the elevator men have to say. Are they all in favour of this? What did their representatives say in the committee? This is the gist of the message. This old grain man talked to the agents himself and found out that they were quite upset about executives in their organizations giving the word on what farmers should believe. The old grain man communicated the following:
Metric meeting held among the pool agents and not with farmers ...
It cannot be denied that Saskatchewan pool elevator men all along the line are against the metric system, and that someone has been misinforming the House.
A week ago I raised a question of privilege, and it was so close to privilege that the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool should have been brought before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. I have here some official resolutions which were passed. I will give the dates, the names which appear on them and so forth, and the House should bear in mind the time frame about which I am talking. The Secretary of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool wrote a letter to the minister which I have here, and which says that during all that period no resolutions were received from the 800 active wheat pool committees, from annual meetings held, or from other membership meetings held throughout the province.
I have here these resolutions on Saskatchewan Wheat Pool stationery. The first one reads:
Re: Federal Government District-Carrot River 14-8
The following resolution was passed at the committee meeting held on February 15, 1977 ...
That was ten days before the secretary wrote his letter to the minister.
... and reported by the secretary of the committee, Mr. Peter Sirey, Box 175, Carrot River, Saskatchewan, and received in head office on February 21, 1977:
That was also before the secretary wrote his letter to the minister, and this is what the resolution says:
Be it resolved that the Carrot River committee is opposed to converting the acre to the hectare.
Carrot River is located in the northeast part of Saskatchewan. This resolution was submitted to the board of directors of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool on February 24, the day before the letter was written.
March 25, 1977

The following is on the same Saskatchewan Wheat Pool stationery. It is from district 13-2 at Burr, in the northwest part of Saskatchewan. It states:
The following resolution was passed at the committee meeting held on February 10, 1977, and reported by the secretary of the committee, Mr. Art Klassen, Burr, Saskatchewan ... and received in head office on February 15, 1977:
That was ten days before the secretary wrote to the minister. The resolution states the following:
That we keep the present system of weights and measurements.
That resolution was submitted to the board of directors on February 17, before the letter was written.
Here is one from a whole district. As hon. members probably know, Saskatchewan is divided into 14 districts under the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool Organization. Each district represents thousands of wheat pool members. This communication reads as follows:
The following resolution was passed at the delegates district meeting held on February 4 and 5, 1977, and was reported by the secretary of the district, Mr. Hugh McDonough,... Cadillac, Sask., and received in head office on February 14, 1977:
That was eleven days before the letter was sent. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale), who is not here, knows where the town of Cadillac is. The people there will not be voting for him the next time around. This resolution reads as follows:
Whereas we understand that there is a possibility that the acre could be changed to hectares we are opposed. We feel that it would be impractical to change the acre as the land is surveyed in acres, and does not coincide or convert equally into any metric form; we also feel that there would be no useful purpose in changing the acre as grain could still be sold in tonnes or kilos per acre rather than per hectare;
Therefore be it resolved that the land area measurement be left as acres.
That was submitted to the board of directors of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool of February 16, 1977, before the secretary wrote the letter.
Here is another one from my district, District 7, Sub-district 4, Grenfell, and it reads as follows:
The following resolution was passed at the committee meeting held on February 24, 1977, and was reported by the secretary of the committee Mr. Donald Crawford, Grenfell, Saskatchewan ... and was received in head office on March 2, 1977:
Whereas there is some difficulty converting miles to kilometres, acres to hectares, and bushels to tonnes, be it resolved that the present acreage system with square miles and bushels be retained. That the railroads change to metric system at the same time as the rest of the grain trade.
This was submitted to J. O. Wright of the board on March 3. 1 will go on and read the one from Avonlea, which is right in the heart of the riding of Assiniboia. It says:
Whereas the metric conversion program is being planned and whereas this program is causing hardship to those of us unfamiliar to the program,
Therefore be it resolved that the program be slowed down until a more effective educational program can be made available.
The hon. member for Assiniboia stood up and said that the secretary of this farm organization is for it, so we all have to
Metric System
accept it. He would not even take the word of the farmers in his own district.
We ask that this conversion be slowed down a little bit. That would make it a little more humane.
Here is one from Plenty in west central Saskatchewan. It is dated February 21 and the resolution reads as follows:
Whereas we are now surveyed in acres and miles, be it resolved that we stay with acres instead of hectares and miles instead of kilometres.
I could go on, but I think I have made my point. In 1970 the government appointed a metric commission to look at the whole thing and to make recommendations to this parliament for legislation. What did the commission do? It went out across the country and told provincial governments and farm organizations that this was the law, that they should get in step, and that the federal government would bring in a bill to be debated here, and in three provinces it became law on February 1, 1977.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw told us that the Metric Commission got the Saskatchewan government to put through an order in council. The Saskatchewan government did not even tell its legislature. Some Saskatchewan cabinet ministers did not even know about it. That order in council changed the whole survey system of Saskatchewan. I have the order in council here, and it says that all surveys, and I quote:
. .. shall be drawn with metric measurements and shall be subject to the approval and inspection, as to their accuracy and the manner in which they are established on the ground, of the Chief Surveyor ...
When a person dies and his estate tries to sell the land and register the title under a new name, there will not only be legal expenses involved but survey expenses as well. The quarter sections in Saskatchewan are not measured accurately. They were measured with a buggy wheel that had a rope tied around it, and that is why our titles say "160 acres more or less." An order in council in Saskatchewan now decrees that measurements must be accurate. That will involve great cost.
I opened my remarks by saying that we are now in the age of metrification without representation. I know what those Saskatchewan farmers will do at the next election. There will be a new government in Saskatchewan. There is going to be a new government here, too.
Ontario accepted the metric system by permissive legislation. Alberta has also passed legislation but has not proclaimed it. I am simply asking members of this government to act like members of parliament instead of allowing themselves to be pushed around by bureaucrats. Stand up and support your people, I say. All we want is that the dual system be left until the farmers accept the new system willingly. We already sell grain under the metric system and there is no quarrel with that. But why make changes that are not necessary? There is no necessity to change the land measurement system, yet the government has told the provinces that it must be done. Then it comes here and blames the whole thing on the provinces.
I ask members of the government to think about what I have been saying, over this weekend. And I suggest that if they do

not think about it they will not be around many more months clouding the atmosphere with the kind of dictatorial nonsense that is contained in this bill.
